analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.59, then in steps to $26.59, and ties it to poverty thresholds.
analysis.headline: A one-member bill to raise the minimum wage to $26.59 by 2030 sits in committee with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $10.59 on January 1, 2026, then add $4 an hour each year until it reaches $26.59 on January 1, 2030. After that, the Department of Labor would reset the wage every seven years so that someone working about 35 hours a week earns at least 40% above the poverty line for a renter family of four with two children. States, cities, and tribes could still set higher minimum wages. It was introduced by a single House member, drew no cosponsors, and was referred to committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, a group concentrated in food service, retail, cleaning, care work, and farming. The bill's stated goal is that a full-time worker can afford basics like rent without falling below the poverty line.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.59 an hour on January 1, 2026, up from the $7.25 that has been in effect since 2009.
Adds $4 an hour each year, reaching $26.59 an hour on January 1, 2030.

After 2030, requires the Department of Labor every seven years to set the wage so that a person working 1,799 hours a year (about 35 hours a week) earns at least 40% above the federal supplemental poverty threshold for a renter family of four with two children.
Bars any downward adjustment: if the formula would produce a lower wage than what is in effect, the current wage stays in place.
Leaves states, cities, territories, and tribes free to set higher minimum wages than the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers would bear higher payroll costs, led by restaurants, retail, hospitality, cleaning, and care providers, some of which would raise prices, automate, or cut hours. Consumers would absorb part of the cost through higher prices. The bill sets no small-business carve-out, no tip-credit or youth-wage phase-in, and no regional adjustment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers and, in part, consumers

drawbacks.text: The increase is steep by any standard: the wage more than triples from $7.25 to $26.59 in five years, with no gradual regional variation or small-business phase-in, which raises the risk of job losses, reduced hours, automation, or faster price increases in low-margin industries.

The post-2030 formula resets the wage only once every seven years, so inflation could erode its real value between adjustments; the 'Sense of Congress' section says the wage should be adjusted whenever inflation rises 5% or more over two years, but that statement does not bind anyone.

The formula is keyed to a national poverty threshold for a family of four, so the same federal minimum would apply in high-cost and low-cost areas alike, understating needs in expensive cities and possibly exceeding local wage levels in cheaper ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers the bill covers, the gain would be direct and large: the current $7.25 federal minimum does not cover fair-market rent for a one-bedroom apartment even with two full-time earners, according to the bill's own findings. The cost side is real but contested: a more-than-tripling of the wage floor over five years, with no regional or small-business cushion, is far more aggressive than recent state-level increases that were phased in over longer periods with local variation, so the risk of reduced hours and faster price increases in low-wage industries would be greater. A more incremental design would have lowered that risk, though it would also have lowered the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It got a committee referral and nothing else: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and so far no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Green (D-TX) introduced the bill in the House on January 3, 2025.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce the same day; no further action has been taken since.

The bill would raise the minimum wage to $10.59 in 2026, then add $4 an hour annually to reach $26.59 in 2030, after which the Department of Labor would reset it every seven years based on the poverty threshold for a renter family of four with two children.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers are better off in the near term: the wage floor stays at $7.25 an hour, where it has stood since 2009, because the bill has not advanced in committee.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2025 and it was referred to committee; he has not attracted any cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; controls whether the bill gets a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the January 3, 2025 referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Chair Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup since it was referred to her committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill has one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of any party, and it sits in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.note: The industry most exposed to a higher wage floor, with a large share of hourly workers below $26.59 and a tip-credit structure the bill does not preserve. Its interest in blocking the bill runs against the wage gains the bill would give its own workers.
Majority-low-wage sectors would face higher payroll costs from the scheduled increases; some of the cost would pass to workers in reduced hours or to consumers in prices.

industries.industry: Home care and child care providers
industries.note: These care sectors employ many low-wage workers who would gain directly, but they are heavily dependent on tight government reimbursement rates and family fees, so a tripling wage floor could squeeze providers and access to care.
A low-wage, labor-intensive sector that would face a much higher federal wage floor; the bill includes no agricultural carve-out.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the session, the realistic path is that the bill dies in the Education and Workforce Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027. Minimum-wage bills from a single minority-party sponsor without committee support do not reach the floor in a chamber controlled by the other party; at most the sponsor could reintroduce it in a future Congress.
